text.title: Node.js Service Layer Architecture Core Rules
text.summary: Seven rules fixing where each concern lives in a Controller-Service-Repository Node.js backend: what a controller may not touch, who owns the transaction, which types cross a layer boundary, where an error becomes an HTTP status, and how the direction of imports is enforced mechanically.

rule.statement: A controller may only parse and validate the request, call exactly one service method, and map the result to a status code plus body. No ORM identifier (`prisma.`, `db.`, `knex`, a model import) may appear anywhere under the controllers directory; enforce it with an ESLint `no-restricted-imports` entry, not by review.

rationale.source: Layered architecture / Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture — Service Layer

rule.rationale: The moment a controller queries directly, the rule it encodes becomes unreachable from the queue worker and the cron job. They copy it, the two copies drift, and the divergence shows up as an invariant that holds over HTTP and not over the worker.

rule.statement: The transaction is opened in the service (`prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...)`) and the `tx` client is passed into every repository call in that unit of work. Repositories MUST accept an optional client parameter and MUST NOT open transactions themselves. Any network call, LLM call or third-party API call is executed outside the transaction callback.

rationale.source: Prisma documentation — interactive transactions (default maxWait 2000 ms, timeout 5000 ms)

rule.rationale: A repository that uses the base client runs its own implicit transaction, so a two-repository unit of work that throws on the second call leaves the first write committed. And an external call inside the callback holds a connection plus row locks for the remote service's latency, so it trips the 5 s interactive-transaction timeout and exhausts the pool under load.

rule.statement: Repository method signatures MUST return domain types declared in the module, not ORM-generated types (`Prisma.UserGetPayload<...>`, `User` imported from `@prisma/client`). No import from the ORM package may appear in a service file.
rule.rationale: A leaked ORM row type puts lazily-shaped fields and nullable columns into the service's contract, so a service test cannot construct an input without the generated types — which means it cannot run without the schema. Swapping Prisma for Drizzle then stops being a repository rewrite and becomes a rewrite of every layer that named the type.

rule.statement: Services throw typed domain errors extending a single base class with a stable `code` (NotFoundError, ConflictError, ValidationError, ForbiddenError). Exactly one error middleware maps code to HTTP status. No `res.` reference and no numeric HTTP status may appear in a service or repository file.

rationale.source: Node.js Error Handling best practices (nodejs.org guide) + Express error-handling middleware

rule.rationale: An HTTP status thrown from a service is meaningless to the queue consumer that shares the same service — it has no response to attach it to and must reverse-map the number back into intent. A single mapping table is what makes the second transport possible at all, and it is the only place a 500 body can be scrubbed of internals.

rule.statement: Every service receives its repositories and external clients as constructor arguments or factory parameters. A service file MUST NOT contain a module-level import of a shared singleton (`import { prisma } from '../db'`, `import { stripe } from '../stripe'`).

rationale.source: Dependency inversion / test-double practice (Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns)

rule.rationale: A module-level singleton is bound at import time, so a test can only replace it through the module registry (`jest.mock` with its hoisting rules). That substitution is process-wide, which makes parallel test files share the double and produces failures that depend on file order rather than on the code under test.

rule.statement: Imports point one way only: controller to service, service to repository. The rule is machine-checked in CI by dependency-cruiser or `eslint-plugin-import/no-restricted-paths`; the artefact names the config file that holds it.

rationale.source: dependency-cruiser — forbidden-dependency rules; Node.js CommonJS cyclic require semantics

rule.rationale: A repository importing a service creates a require cycle. Under CommonJS the second module in the cycle receives a partially initialised exports object, so a class comes back `undefined` — and whether it breaks depends on which entry point was loaded first, so it passes in tests and fails in the worker.

rule.statement: Skip when the service is a BFF that only forwards to another API with no business rules of its own, or when exactly one transport (HTTP) will ever call the logic and no second consumer is planned. Emit a structured skip naming which condition held.
rule.rationale: The layering pays for itself by making one rule reachable from several transports and testable without a database. With a single transport and no domain rules the layers add indirection and a file count with nothing on the other side of the trade.
